title: 5. Leading Operational KPIs, Structural Potential & CEO Walk-the-Talk
book_title: Chapter 5: The Operator's Scorecard — Leading KPIs & Haviv Ilan's Execution

epigraph.quote: Our North Star has never changed: long-term growth of free cash flow per share.
epigraph.author: Haviv Ilan, President & CEO, Texas Instruments

web_blocks.html: Texas Instruments runs its business around 20-year factory assets, not quarterly fab-load optics. Judging management therefore requires tracking six leading operational KPIs across the cycle [4]. Read together through Q3 2026, these six metrics tell a clear story. They show why the 2023–2025 trough looked strained, and why the 2026 rebound marks a real structural turn [1, 2, 4].

web_blocks.takeaway: Five of six operational KPIs turned decisively positive in 2026, while inventory days (194) and Embedded Processing margin recovery (26.5%) remain active watch items.

web_blocks.html: CEO Walk-the-Talk Audit (Haviv Ilan, 2023–2026): Haviv Ilan became CEO in April 2023, just as industrial and auto buyers cut orders [4, 7]. At the same time, TI committed to $5 billion a year in fab capex [4, 7]. Critics asked if management would burn cash indefinitely on empty cleanrooms. Three years later, the record shows what Ilan delivered and what new risks he took on:

• Delivered — Sherman SM1 & Modular Pacing: TI started initial output at SM1 in December 2025 on schedule and finished the SM2 shell [4]. That removed multi-year build delays so future tool installs can match real order growth [4].
  • Delivered — CapEx Step-Down & CHIPS Act Finalization: Management cut peak spending as promised, guiding 2026 capex to $2.0B–$3.0B ($2,578M TTM through Q3 2026) [2, 4]. It also locked in $1.6B in direct CHIPS grants and $630M in direct grant receipts through Q3 2026 alongside the OBBBA-enhanced 35% ITC for post-2025 equipment [1, 2, 4, 5].
  • Delivered — Inventory Discipline Without Fire Sales: TI refused to dump wafers at cut-rate prices during 2024. It held pricing firm and worked DIO down from 241 days at end-2024 to 222 days at end-2025 and 194 days in Q3 2026 [1, 2]. Meanwhile, Q3 2026 sales grew +28% year-over-year [2].
  • New Execution Test — $7.5B Silicon Labs Integration: In February 2026, Ilan pivoted from pure organic builds to a $7.5B all-cash deal for Silicon Labs, targeting an H1 2027 close [6]. TI plans to move Silicon Labs' wireless IoT wafers from outside foundries into LFAB in Utah and Sherman in Texas [6]. Qualifying and moving ~1,200 wireless parts onto internal 28nm–65nm lines without losing sockets will test Ilan from 2027 to 2029.

Management Commentary & Guidance Execution (Q2–Q3 2026): On the October 21, 2026 Q3 earnings call, CEO Haviv Ilan summed up the demand turn: "Secular growth of semiconductor content is continuing alongside a strong cyclical recovery." [2] He tied that rebound directly to TI's fab footprint: "Our cash flow from operations of $9.9 billion for the trailing 12 months again underscored the strength of our business model, the quality of our product portfolio and the benefit of 300mm production. Free cash flow for the same period was $8.4 billion." [2] That beat followed steady guidance discipline across TI's CFO transition. Before Julie Knecht succeeded Rafael Lizardi as CFO on August 1, 2026, Lizardi guided Q3 on the Q2 call: "We expect TI's revenue in the range of $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and earnings per share to be in the range of $2.23 to $2.57." [3] Actual Q3 2026 results hit $6.055B in revenue and $2.62 in EPS, topping the EPS ceiling on stronger fab utilization [2]. For Q4 2026, management guided revenue of $5.80 billion to $6.30 billion and EPS of $2.45 to $2.79, signaling seasonal steadiness after Q3's surge [2]. Meanwhile, Form 4 filings from October 27 through November 13, 2026 showed only routine option exercises and same-day sales by five non-employee directors (6,065 to 8,758 shares each) with zero C-suite open-market selling.

Structural Potential Through 2030: RFAB2 is ramping, SM1 is in early production, and SM2 and LFAB2 shells stand ready for modular tools [1, 4]. Meanwhile, Data Center has grown into a 9% end market [1]. By 2030, TI aims to build >95% of its wafers in-house, mostly on 300mm lines [4]. Those sites support $24B–$28B+ in annual revenue capacity against $2B–$3B in steady-state capex [4]. At that scale, normalized free-cash-flow margins sit far above the 8%–17% trough seen in 2023–2025.

Why Data Center & Edge AI Power Matter to the 2030 Capacity Math: Rising AI server rack power is a key driver behind TI's 2026 fab-load rebound [1, 4]. Cloud clusters are shifting from 12V to 48V power rails to feed 100kW+ racks. Each server now needs more multiphase controllers, smart power stages, hot-swap eFuses, and isolated gate drivers. Even at 9% of FY2025 sales, Data Center is TI's fastest-growing end market [1, 2]. Alongside industrial and auto recovery, it helps fill 300mm wafer lines at RFAB2 and SM1 [1, 2].

Operating Expense Leverage & Margin Elasticity: TI's fixed R&D and SG&A base creates a second margin lever in 2026 [1, 2]. In FY2025, TI spent $2,083 million on R&D and $1,860 million on SG&A, or ~22.3% of sales combined [1]. Direct TI.com sales and an 80,000-part catalog scale without linear staff growth. When quarterly sales rose from $4,825 million in Q1 2026 to $6,055 million in Q3 2026, operating margin jumped 1,000 basis points—from 37.5% to 47.5%—in two quarters [2, 3].

2027–2028 Fab Utilization & Silicon Labs Migration Milestones: Management's credibility over the next two years rests on two clear tests. First, TI must bring Days of Inventory down from 194 days toward 150–170 days without hurting direct lead times [2, 4]. Second, it must transfer Silicon Labs' 1,200 wireless IoT parts from outside foundries to internal 300mm lines after the H1 2027 close [6]. Keeping gross capex inside the $2B–$3B band during those transfers will prove that TI's modular fab plan works [4].

Long-Term FCF-per-Share Scorecard: TI ties executive pay and capital choices directly to long-term growth in free cash flow per share, not raw market share [4]. Most 300mm cleanroom shells are now built, and CHIPS Act incentives cut net capital cost [4, 5]. As a result, each new dollar of industrial, auto, and data-center sales converts to cash at a high rate [2, 4].

Embedded Processing Recovery & Inventory-Margin Divergence: Two subtle signals in Q3 2026 confirm that TI's turnaround is healthy. First, Embedded Processing margin jumped from 11.3% in FY2025 to 26.5% in Q3 2026, showing that prior weakness stemmed from Lehi fab startup costs rather than lost sockets [1, 2]. Second, Days of Inventory fell from 241 days in 2024 to 194 days in Q3 2026 while gross margin climbed to 64.2% [1, 2]. Falling inventory alongside rising gross margin proves real end-customer demand is absorbing factory output.

Modular Cleanroom Pacing & Capital Flexibility: One of the biggest operational upgrades from the 2022–2025 buildout is how TI now adds capacity [4]. Before building SM1, SM2, and LFAB2, adding cleanroom space meant waiting three years for concrete, steel, and power hookups. Today, the heavy shells are built or advancing on schedule [4]. Management can keep cleanroom bays idle and install wafer tools only when customer orders justify the spend [4]. That shift turns capex from a multi-year fixed commitment into a responsive valve.

What Could Trip Up the 2027–2028 Scorecard: Even with strong 2026 momentum, two operational risks deserve close tracking. First, if industrial or automotive demand slows again before DIO reaches 150–170 days, TI could face another period of under-absorbed fab depreciation [1, 2]. Second, moving 1,200 Silicon Labs wireless parts off external foundries onto internal 28nm–65nm lines requires strict yield and customer-qualification discipline [6]. Smooth execution on both fronts will confirm whether Haviv Ilan's operating model delivers lasting owner earnings.

web_blocks.title: THE 2027–2028 EXECUTION CHECKLIST
paragraphs: Track three leading signals over the next eight quarters: (1) DIO falling from 194 days toward 150–170 days while gross margin stays above 60%; (2) Embedded Processing margin holding above 25% and moving toward 30%+ after Silicon Labs closes; and (3) gross capex staying inside the $2B–$3B band unless demand justifies new cleanroom tools.

book_paragraphs: Once you know how a company makes money, the next step is checking whether management walks the talk. You do not need fifty metrics to grade Texas Instruments. Six leading operational KPIs tell the whole story quarter by quarter.

First is Gross Margin. In 2025, heavy 300mm depreciation and startup costs pulled gross margin down to 57.0%. By Q3 2026, higher volume and fuller fabs pushed gross margin back up to 64.2%—a 720-basis-point gain. Second is Direct Channel Share, which now tops 80% including TI.com. That direct link gives TI clean demand signals and cuts out middleman margin leakage.

Third is Days of Inventory. TI's stock peaked at 241 days at end-2024, eased to 222 days at end-2025, and fell to 194 days ($4.7 billion) in Q3 2026. That path moves in the right direction, though 194 days stays on our watch list. Fourth is Gross CapEx. After spending $5.07 billion in 2023, $4.82 billion in 2024, and $4.55 billion in 2025, TI stepped down to its $2.0 billion to $3.0 billion 2026 plan, with Q3 capex at just $463 million.

Fifth is Embedded Processing operating margin, which fell from 38.4% in 2022 to 11.3% in 2025 before bouncing to 26.5% in Q3 2026. Sixth is CHIPS Act and OBBBA execution. TI signed up to $1.6 billion in direct grant deals ($630 million collected through Q3 2026) and now captures a 35% Investment Tax Credit under the 2025 One Big Beautiful Bill Act, lifting nine-month 2026 CHIPS cash benefits to $1,484 million. For Q4 2026, management guided revenue of $5.80 billion to $6.30 billion and EPS of $2.45 to $2.79, while October–November 2026 Form 4 filings showed only routine non-employee director option exercises.

book_subsections.title: Grading Haviv Ilan's Walk-the-Talk
paragraphs: Haviv Ilan took over as CEO in April 2023 just as the analog cycle turned down and capex hit $5 billion a year. Three years later, his organic report card is strong. Sherman's SM1 fab entered early output on schedule in December 2025, and SM2's shell is done. Capex stepped down as promised, and TI never dumped parts at fire-sale prices to clear stock.

Management's own words on the October 21, 2026 Q3 call capture that turn clearly. CEO Haviv Ilan stated: "Secular growth of semiconductor content is continuing alongside a strong cyclical recovery." He then linked the recovery directly to TI's 300mm factories: "Our cash flow from operations of $9.9 billion for the trailing 12 months again underscored the strength of our business model, the quality of our product portfolio and the benefit of 300mm production. Free cash flow for the same period was $8.4 billion."

Guidance execution held steady right through TI's CFO transition as well. Before Julie Knecht succeeded Rafael Lizardi as CFO on August 1, 2026, Lizardi gave Q3 guidance on the Q2 call: "We expect TI's revenue in the range of $5.65 billion to $6.15 billion and earnings per share to be in the range of $2.23 to $2.57." Actual Q3 2026 results delivered $6.055 billion in revenue and $2.62 in EPS, beating the top of that earnings range.

Now Ilan has placed a big new bet: the $7.5 billion cash deal for Silicon Labs, due to close in H1 2027. Moving 1,200 wireless IoT parts onto TI's 300mm Lehi and Sherman lines fits the National Semiconductor playbook. Silicon Labs brings low-power Bluetooth, Zigbee, Thread, Matter, and Wi-Fi chips that pair cleanly with TI's C2000 and MSPM0 microcontrollers.

Even so, moving wafers from outside foundries to internal fabs is tricky work. Shifting 1,200 mixed-signal wireless parts onto TI's 28nm–65nm lines requires fresh customer testing in factories and smart buildings. Moving those wafers smoothly without losing sockets—while keeping capex inside $2B–$3B—will define Ilan's next three years.

Look also at the revenue headroom TI has built. Between RFAB1, RFAB2, LFAB1, and SM1—plus modular shells at SM2 and LFAB2—TI has enough cleanroom space for $24 billion to $28 billion or more in yearly sales over the next decade. It will not need to break ground on another greenfield site. New sales from factory gear, electric cars, and 48-volt AI server racks now drop through to operating profit at high margins.

In the end, grading Haviv Ilan comes down to capital discipline. During the slump, he held firm on 300mm builds, and in 2026 he cut capex right on cue. If he now works inventory below 180 days and runs a clean Silicon Labs fab move in 2027–2028, TI's free cash flow per share will reach a higher plateau.

Another metric worth watching alongside inventory days is R&D and SG&A leverage. In FY2025, TI spent $2,083 million on R&D and $1,860 million on SG&A, or 22.3% of sales combined. Because TI sells mostly direct and its analog R&D creates long-lived parts, operating costs grow much slower than sales in an upturn. When quarterly sales rose from $4.83 billion in Q1 2026 to $6.06 billion in Q3 2026, operating margin jumped 10 full points from 37.5% to 47.5%.

Also put the Embedded Processing rebound in context. For two years, critics feared TI's 11.3% Embedded margin in FY2025 meant permanent share loss to NXP, STMicroelectronics, or Renesas. The Q3 2026 jump to 26.5% ($227 million profit on $858 million sales) proves the dip came mainly from Lehi startup costs and low fab load. Embedded still sits below its 38% 2022 peak, yet the turn is clear.

Tracking capex discipline through 2027 and 2028 matters just as much. Management set $2 billion to $3 billion as the new yearly capex band now that heavy shells at RFAB2, SM1, SM2, and LFAB2 are built or advancing on schedule. Watching capex stay in that $2B–$3B band as annual sales climb toward $21 billion to $24 billion is the cleanest test of Ilan's FCF-per-share North Star.

Finally, watch how inventory days and gross margin move together. In Q3 2026, TI cut Days of Inventory to 194 days ($4.7 billion) while raising gross margin to 64.2%. Falling inventory days paired with rising gross margin is the gold standard of chip-cycle health. It proves real end-buyer orders—not channel stuffing—are filling TI's fabs. As long as DIO trends toward 150–170 days with gross margin above 60%, TI's scorecard stays strong.

Also notice how modular cleanroom pacing changes TI's risk profile from 2027 onward. Before 2022, expanding wafer capacity meant waiting three years to pour concrete and wire high-voltage substations. With SM2 in Sherman and LFAB2 in Utah advancing on schedule, those heavy shells are already in place. Management can leave empty bays unequipped until demand warrants buying tools, keeping annual capex disciplined.

That operational flexibility also supports TI's dividend and buyback engine over a full cycle. Because executive pay is tied to long-term growth in free cash flow per share, management has no incentive to chase low-margin volume just to boost headline sales. Every decision—from holding firm on pricing in 2024 to pacing cleanroom tooling in 2026—points back to compounding cash per share.

Keep those six operational KPIs front and center as 2027 unfolds. When gross margin stays above 60%, inventory trends toward 150 to 170 days, and capex remains inside the $2 billion to $3 billion band, the numbers prove that Haviv Ilan's strategy is working in real time. Combined with a smooth Silicon Labs wafer transfer into Lehi and Sherman, those metrics turn a multi-year fab buildout into durable owner earnings. If any of those three guardrails slips, careful investors will spot the shift in the quarterly scorecard long before it hits the annual dividend or share buybacks.

book_callouts.title: NARRATOR'S REFLECTION
book_callouts.text: Management earned trust by finishing the heavy 300mm shells and cutting capex in 2026 as promised. The two open tests—working inventory below 180 days and moving Silicon Labs wafers in-house in 2027—are execution tasks, not existential risks.
